task-effects.kicker: The task framework · a conceptual map
task-effects.title: One technology. Three effects on workers.
task-effects.intro: These forces can operate together. The outcome depends on their strength, not on moving from one box to the next.
task-effects.takeaway: More output does not automatically mean more income for workers. Ask which tasks disappear, which remain, and which are created.

cards.label: Displacement
cards.title: Machines take over tasks
cards.text: Work previously done by people moves to capital. Demand for labor in those tasks falls.

cards.label: Productivity
cards.title: Remaining work can expand
cards.text: Lower production costs can increase output and demand for people in tasks that remain.

cards.label: Reinstatement
cards.title: New tasks need people
cards.text: New work creates roles where labor has a comparative advantage.

task-effects.question: Which effects dominate?

outcomes.title: Gains reach workers
outcomes.text: Productivity gains and new tasks are strong enough to support labor demand and wages.

outcomes.title: “So-so” automation
outcomes.text: Tasks are displaced, with too little productivity gain or new work to compensate.

sources: Acemoglu & Restrepo, Automation and New Tasks (2019)

labor-share.kicker: An illustrative example · not measured data
labor-share.title: Getting another job can still mean a smaller share.
labor-share.intro: Hold output at $100 to isolate the direct effect. Move a $10 task from labor to capital; then ask what could offset the loss.
labor-share.takeaway: Employment, wages, and labor’s share are different outcomes. A recovery in jobs alone does not establish that wages or labor’s share recovered.

offsets.title: Expansion in remaining tasks
offsets.text: Lower costs can expand output and increase demand for people who still do part of the work.

offsets.title: Creation of new tasks
offsets.text: New products and activities can create work that people are better placed to do.

labor-share.note: The later response is not assigned a number here. It can offset part, all, or more than the initial loss; this example holds everything else fixed.
sources: Model context: Automation and New Tasks (2019)

education-outliers.kicker: A guide to mechanisms · not a fitted regression
education-outliers.title: Skills matter. So does the route from skills to income.
education-outliers.intro: These are explanations to investigate when educational performance and economic outcomes diverge. They are not a ranking of countries.
education-outliers.takeaway: A genuine outlier chart needs a defined outcome, comparable test years, and a fitted model. GDP per person and GDP growth answer different questions.

rows.label: Skills put to use
rows.title: Learning can support production
rows.mechanism: People can apply their skills in firms and markets.
rows.result: A route from skills to economic gains

rows.label: Skills face barriers
rows.title: Potential may go unrealized
rows.mechanism: Weak institutions, limited market access, or migration can interrupt that route.
rows.result: A possible explanation for lower output

rows.label: Income has other sources
rows.title: Resources can lift income
rows.mechanism: Oil, gas, or other resource rents add income beyond what test scores measure.
rows.result: A possible explanation for higher income

education-outliers.note: The examples in this article are illustrative. No residual analysis has been reproduced, so this figure does not certify any named country as an outlier.
sources: Hanushek & Woessmann, The Knowledge Capital of Nations

community-rights.kicker: Community elbow room · the book’s two layers
community-rights.title: Different choices. A common floor of rights.
community-rights.intro: Local self-government allows communities to pursue different priorities. Individual freedoms set the limit on that discretion.
community-rights.takeaway: A community can hold views you reject. In this account, it cannot turn those views into restrictions that take away basic individual freedoms.

innovation-lineage.kicker: An intellectual history · dates are not to scale
innovation-lineage.title: Scarcity changes what is worth inventing.
innovation-lineage.intro: Follow one question through the literature: when labor becomes scarce or expensive, does innovation turn toward saving it?
innovation-lineage.takeaway: Incentives can redirect technology. They do not guarantee that every society will adapt, or that the benefits will be shared.
innovation-lineage.source_mermaid:
timeline
    title Induced innovation
    1932 : Hicks, The Theory of Wages : "A change in relative prices is itself a spur to invention"
    1962 : Habakkuk : Scarce American labor drove American mechanization
    1964-1966 : Kennedy, Samuelson, Drandakis-Phelps : Formal induced-innovation models
    1969 : Kamien and Schwartz : Critiques; the literature stalls
    1998-2002 : Acemoglu, Directed Technical Change : The modern revival, with microfoundations
    2018-2022 : Acemoglu and Restrepo, Demographics and Automation : Aging causes automation - and that is fine
    2026 : Acemoglu, Autor, Beirne and Scott : Baby Busts and Growth Booms

groups.title: The intuition and the early models

rows.title: Hicks · The Theory of Wages
rows.text: Relative factor prices can influence the direction of invention.

rows.title: Habakkuk · American and British Technology
rows.text: A historical argument: scarce American labor encouraged mechanization. The thesis remains contested.

rows.title: Kennedy, Samuelson, Drandakis & Phelps
rows.text: Formal models turn induced innovation from a historical intuition into an economic mechanism.

rows.title: Kamien & Schwartz
rows.text: Further modeling of induced technical progress.

rows.title: Acemoglu · Directed technical change
rows.text: Market size and relative prices help explain which technologies innovators develop.

rows.title: Acemoglu & Restrepo · Demographics and Automation
rows.text: From working paper to publication: aging is associated with more automation. Productivity effects depend on the setting.

rows.title: Acemoglu, Autor, Beirne & Scott · Baby Busts and Growth Booms
rows.text: The paper Cowen invokes when asking whether fewer young workers can induce a technological response.

sources: Acemoglu, Factor Prices and Technical Change: review of the earlier literature

ai-clocks.kicker: Historical windows and a forecast horizon
ai-clocks.title: A short boom can sit inside a long wait.
ai-clocks.intro: Cowen emphasizes the years when gains become visible. Acemoglu emphasizes the investment and organizational change before those gains arrive.
ai-clocks.takeaway: Choose the time window before comparing the claim. And keep productivity gains, GDP gains, and annual growth rates in separate columns.
ai-clocks.source_mermaid:
timeline
    title Whose clock is running?
    1975-1995 : Two decades of IT investment : Little measured productivity gain : "Computers everywhere but in the statistics"
    1995-1998 : The boom : Productivity growth up ~0.5 pp : Cowen's benchmark
    2004-2019 : Productivity slowdown : Despite continued IT investment
    2022-2026 : LLM capability rises fast : Application layer lags : Acemoglu's "sluggish diffusion"
    2026-2036 : The disputed decade : Acemoglu +0.05pp : Cowen +0.5pp : Industry +1.5pp or more

groups.title: The IT precedent, as this conversation frames it

rows.title: Investment before the payoff
rows.text: The long preparation period in Acemoglu’s reading: adoption and reorganization take time.

rows.title: The boom Cowen points to
rows.text: A short window of visible improvement becomes his benchmark for what AI might deliver.

rows.title: The later slowdown
rows.text: Continued investment does not imply a permanently faster rate of productivity growth.

groups.title: AI: separate what is happening from what is assumed

rows.title: Capability versus diffusion
rows.text: The interview distinguishes fast model improvement from slower development of useful applications.

rows.title: This page’s illustrative scenario window
rows.text: The arithmetic table holds chosen GDP-growth increments constant for ten years. Its rows are not forecasts attributed to the interviewees or to Goldman Sachs. The source table above preserves each estimate's own measure and horizon.

ai-clocks.note: Total-factor productivity (TFP) and GDP are different measures. Acemoglu’s 2024 paper reports separate ten-year gains; neither can be substituted directly for an annual GDP-growth rate.

social-contracts.kicker: A map of arguments · not a chain of succession
social-contracts.title: Change the starting point. Change the agreement.
social-contracts.intro: These thinkers use different kinds of agreement to answer different questions. Read across each entry: the premise helps explain the conclusion.
social-contracts.takeaway: The question behind Acemoglu’s objection: when does an argument about what people would accept become a substitute for asking actual people?
social-contracts.source_mermaid:
timeline
    title The social contract lineage
    1651 : Hobbes, Leviathan : Absolute sovereign; the alternative is war of all against all
    1689 : Locke, Two Treatises : Government by consent; rights precede the state; revolution permitted
    1762 : Rousseau, Du contrat social : The general will; "forced to be free"
    1785 : Kant : The contract as a regulative idea, not a historical event
    1971 : Rawls, A Theory of Justice : Original position, veil of ignorance
    1974 : Nozick, Anarchy State and Utopia : Minimal state from the same starting point
    1986 : Gauthier, Morals by Agreement : Contract from rational bargaining
    1998 : Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other : Principles nobody could reasonably reject

rows.title: Hobbes · Leviathan
rows.premise: People need security against violent conflict.

rows.title: Locke · Two Treatises
rows.premise: People have rights before government exists.
rows.result: Government is limited and must protect those rights.

rows.title: Rousseau · The Social Contract
rows.premise: Citizens associate under a general will aimed at the common good.

rows.title: Kant · Theory and Practice
rows.premise: The original contract is an idea of reason, not a historical event.
rows.result: Laws should be tested against possible public consent.

rows.title: Rawls · A Theory of Justice
rows.premise: Choose principles without knowing your place in society.
rows.result: Fair terms for the basic structure of society.

rows.title: Nozick · Anarchy, State, and Utopia
rows.premise: Individual rights constrain what others and the state may do.
rows.result: A minimal state; a rival to Rawls, not the same contract argument.

rows.title: Gauthier · Morals by Agreement
rows.premise: Rational bargainers seek mutually advantageous cooperation.

rows.title: Scanlon · What We Owe to Each Other
rows.premise: Ask which principles no one could reasonably reject.
rows.result: A test of moral justification, not a blueprint for the state.

sources: Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other
